```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A smooth describes a relationship without requiring it to be linear. {glmmTMB}
can estimate these relationships alongside its other model components, and
{gratia} can extract and display their effects. The examples below ask how
annual river flow changes over time and how plants respond to increasing carbon
dioxide concentration. The second example also accounts for measurements on
the same plant.

This article needs the optional package glmmTMB, with support for `mgcv::s()`
terms; the examples require glmmTMB 1.1.15.2 or later and {mgcv} 1.9-4.
Smooth fitting remains experimental in glmmTMB. Its
[fitting documentation](https://glmmtmb.github.io/glmmTMB/reference/glmmTMB.html)
recommends `REML = TRUE`. Attach mgcv and write `s()` in the model formula so
glmmTMB can recognise the smooth and estimate its smoothing penalty. We also
load {ggplot2} to plot the data and predictions.

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library("gratia")
load_mgcv()
library("glmmTMB")
library("ggplot2")
```

## Fit a smooth trend in annual river flow

The [Nile data](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/datasets/html/Nile.html)
contain 100 annual flow measurements at Aswan from 1871 to 1970, measured in
units of $10^8$ cubic metres. The question here is descriptive: what broad
change in mean flow is supported by these observations? We adapt the smooth
example in the glmmTMB documentation, name the variables `year` and `flow`, and
fit the same spline with mgcv for comparison.

```{r nile-data}
nile <- data.frame(
  year = as.numeric(time(Nile)),
  flow = as.numeric(Nile)
)
ggplot(nile, aes(year, flow)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = expression(Annual ~ flow ~ (10^8 ~ m^3)))
```

Annual flow is continuous. A Gaussian model is a reasonable starting point for
departures around a smooth mean, provided its residual spread is reasonably
stable. The observations are a time series, so independence needs checking;
year appearing in a smooth does not itself model residual serial dependence.
Fit the same Gaussian smooth with mgcv and glmmTMB so we can compare the
extracted effects and predictions.

```{r nile-fit}
nile_gam <- gam(flow ~ s(year, k = 10), data = nile, method = "REML")
nile_tmb <- glmmTMB(flow ~ s(year, k = 10), data = nile,
  family = gaussian(), REML = TRUE, start = list(theta = 5))
summary(nile_tmb)
```

`k = 10` sets the size of the spline basis. The fitted penalty determines how
much the curve can bend within that basis. The `start` argument supplies an
initial log standard deviation for the spline's random coefficients, which
glmmTMB estimates during fitting. The `dummy` random effect in the summary
represents those spline coefficients.

## Extract the smooth and its uncertainty

List the available smooths with `smooths()`, then extract the year effect with
`smooth_estimates()`. Save the estimates so they can be inspected and passed
to `draw()` without evaluating the model again.

```{r nile-extraction}
smooths(nile_tmb)
head(smooth_coefs(nile_tmb, select = "s(year)"))
trend <- smooth_estimates(nile_tmb, select = "s(year)",
  interval = "credible")
head(trend)
draw(trend, xlab = "Year", ylab = expression(Flow ~ contribution ~ (10^8 ~ m^3)))
```

The curve shows the smooth's contribution to expected flow. In this model a
positive value means that expected flow is above the fitted intercept. The
broad decline around the turn of the twentieth century is clearer than the
smaller changes that follow. The shaded region shows uncertainty in the
estimated trend at each year and includes uncertainty in the intercept by
default.

The interval uses glmmTMB's covariance for the fitted coefficients, including
covariance between fixed and random coefficients. The mgcv covariance options
`frequentist = TRUE` and `unconditional = TRUE` are unavailable for glmmTMB
effects.

At any particular year a pointwise interval is useful. If the claim concerns
the entire plotted trend, ask for a simultaneous band instead:

```{r nile-simultaneous}
draw(nile_tmb, select = "s(year)", interval = "simultaneous",
  n = 120, n_sim = 3000, seed = 71,
  xlab = "Year", ylab = expression(Flow ~ contribution ~ (10^8 ~ m^3)))
```

The wider band is designed to cover the trend jointly across the years where
the smooth was evaluated. The earlier `interval = "credible"` is an alias for
the pointwise option, `interval = "confidence"`. For mgcv models, choose
`frequentist = TRUE` to change the covariance used to calculate either type
of interval.

For the full expected flow, add the intercept. Here the model has just one
smooth and an identity link, so this gives a direct comparison with both
packages' predictions:

```{r nile-predictions}
year_grid <- data.frame(year = seq(1871, 1970, length.out = 120))
full_trend <- smooth_estimates(nile_tmb, data = year_grid,
  interval = "credible")
full_trend$mean_flow <- full_trend$.estimate + unname(fixef(nile_tmb)$cond[1])
full_trend$lower <- full_trend$.lower_ci + unname(fixef(nile_tmb)$cond[1])
full_trend$upper <- full_trend$.upper_ci + unname(fixef(nile_tmb)$cond[1])
full_trend$mgcv_mean <- as.numeric(predict(nile_gam, newdata = year_grid))
ggplot(full_trend, aes(year, mean_flow)) +
  geom_point(data = nile, aes(y = flow), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_line(aes(y = mgcv_mean), colour = "steelblue", linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = expression(Annual ~ flow ~ (10^8 ~ m^3)),
    subtitle = "glmmTMB mean and interval; dashed blue line is the mgcv mean")
```

`overall_uncertainty = TRUE`, the default, includes uncertainty in the model
constant in the smooth's standard errors. Adding the intercept to the displayed
values therefore gives appropriate mean intervals for this one-smooth model.
For a model with several terms, adding only the intercept would leave out the
other contributions; use predictions from the full model instead. The two
mean curves almost coincide here because the models use the same Gaussian
likelihood and spline penalty. Such agreement is not expected automatically
for non-Gaussian fits or more complex random-effect structures.

For the mgcv fit, we can compare the two covariance choices at years of
interest while leaving the estimated trend unchanged:

```{r nile-covariance-choices}
comparison_years <- data.frame(year = c(1880, 1920))
bayesian_effect <- smooth_estimates(nile_gam, data = comparison_years)
frequentist_effect <- smooth_estimates(nile_gam, data = comparison_years,
  frequentist = TRUE, interval = "confidence")
data.frame(year = comparison_years$year,
  contribution = bayesian_effect$.estimate,
  bayesian_se = bayesian_effect$.se,
  frequentist_se = frequentist_effect$.se)
gam_covariance <- get_vcov(nile_gam, frequentist = TRUE)
```

The frequentist covariance describes how the estimated coefficients would
vary across repeated samples with the smoothing parameters held fixed. Its
standard errors describe sampling variation and can be small even when
smoothing pulls the estimate away from the true curve. The default for
smooth-effect intervals is the approximate Bayesian covariance. Use
`get_vcov()` to extract the covariance for your own calculations.

## Check residual variation and serial correlation

Use `appraise()` to compare the residual distribution with simulations from
the fitted model. Then use `residual_correlation_plot()` to look for similar
departures in successive years, which the independent Gaussian errors do not
represent.

```{r nile-checks}
appraise(nile_tmb, type = "pearson", method = "simulate",
  n_simulate = 100, seed = 72)
residual_correlation_plot(nile_tmb, type = "pearson", lag_max = 15)
```

The panel uses glmmTMB's Pearson residuals. For this Gaussian fit they
remain on the scale of the flow response, rather than standard-normal scores.
Simulated QQ references hold the fitted smooth fixed and generate new
annual responses. They check the response distribution under this fitted
model; they do not refit the trend. The separate autocorrelation plot asks
whether successive departures still resemble one another. Its correlations
describe ordered residual structure, with no significance bands that assume
independent residuals. Lags are observation positions; here each position
corresponds to one year.

Most of the QQ points follow their simulated reference, with the lowest-flow
observation standing out in the lower tail. The serial-correlation plot checks
whether neighbouring years have similar departures from that distribution.

The residual correlation at lag one is about 0.24, with much smaller correlation
at lag two. Some adjacent-year structure remains after removing the smooth
trend. A time-series model can represent that remaining correlation when
estimating trend uncertainty. The smooth describes a broad decline in
mean flow, while the residual check identifies variation that its independent
Gaussian errors leave unexplained. See
[the model diagnostics article](model-checking.html) for checks of
dependence and for the distinction between holding effects fixed, drawing
their uncertainty and simulating new effects.

## Plot smooth and random effects for repeated plant measurements

The `CO2` experiment recorded carbon dioxide uptake by twelve plants of
*Echinochloa crus-galli* at seven concentrations. The researchers paired
plants within each origin (Quebec or Mississippi). One plant in each pair
received the chilling treatment and the other served as a control. Table 1
of the [original study](https://biology.mcgill.ca/faculty/potvin/articles/PotvinLech_90.pdf)
gives concentrations in $\mu\mathrm{L}\,\mathrm{L}^{-1}$. We use these data to
illustrate repeated measurements, with a Gamma model to let the variance of
positive uptake increase with its mean.

We use a shared smooth response to concentration, an origin-by-treatment
interaction and plant-specific intercepts and slopes. The shared smooth
describes the curved response, and the slopes allow plants to differ in
their response to concentration. The model accounts for repeated measurements
within each plant. The treatment terms illustrate how to plot an interaction
in this fit, which omits the pairing used in the experiment.

```{r plant-data-model}
plant <- as.data.frame(CO2)
plant$Plant <- factor(plant$Plant, ordered = FALSE)
plant$log_conc <- log(plant$conc) - mean(log(plant$conc))
plant_tmb <- glmmTMB(
  uptake ~ Type * Treatment + s(log_conc, k = 5) + (1 + log_conc | Plant),
  data = plant, family = Gamma(link = "log"), REML = TRUE)
summary(plant_tmb)
```

For non-Gaussian responses, glmmTMB recommends simulations for the intended
design to check REML estimates and interval coverage.

Each plant's random intercept gives its departure from the shared predictor at
the geometric mean concentration, where `log_conc` is zero. The shared curve
represents rapid change at low concentrations and slower change at high
concentrations. The interaction allows the treatment difference in log mean
uptake to vary by origin.

Plot the model effects to see the shared concentration curve, treatment
contributions, and differences between plants in one figure.

```{r plant-effects, fig.height = 9}
draw(plant_tmb, ncol = 2)
```

`draw()` includes smooths, random effects and parametric effects by
default. The Gaussian QQ panels for plant intercepts and slopes show fitted
plant deviations, not response residuals. The random coefficients that encode
the spline are excluded from these panels. `parametric = FALSE` omits
parametric panels; an explicit `select` draws only selected effects unless
`parametric = TRUE` is also supplied. To see each plant's combined intercept
and slope contribution, select both random-effect terms and set
`ranef_lines = TRUE`.

```{r plant-random-lines}
draw(plant_tmb, select = c("(1 | Plant)", "(log_conc | Plant)"),
  ranef_lines = TRUE)
```

Each line shows plant $j$'s departure from the shared predictor,
$b_{0j} + x b_{1j}$, where $x$ is the centred log concentration. This display
requires an intercept and a single numeric slope in the same formula term.
Terms with multiple slopes, transformed or factor slopes, or structured
covariance use separate QQ panels.

Use `parametric_effects()` to isolate the origin-by-treatment interaction.
This shows how treatment differences vary between the two origins.

```{r plant-parametric-interaction}
parametric_terms(plant_tmb)
draw(parametric_effects(plant_tmb, terms = "Type:Treatment"))
```

These are contrast-coded partial contributions on the log scale. Contrast
coding gives the reference category a zero contribution; full predictions add
the intercept and the other model terms. Parametric intervals include
intercept uncertainty and its covariance with the term by default; use
`overall_uncertainty = FALSE` for uncertainty in the term alone. The estimated
partial contributions do not change. Full predictions combine all terms:

```{r plant-full-predictions}
plant$expected <- as.numeric(predict(plant_tmb, type = "response"))
ggplot(plant, aes(conc, uptake, group = Plant, colour = Treatment)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(aes(y = expected)) +
  facet_wrap(~ Type) +
  labs(x = expression(CO[2] ~ concentration ~ (mu * L ~ L^{-1})),
    y = expression(CO[2] ~ uptake ~ (mu * mol ~ m^{-2} ~ s^{-1})))
```

The curves describe these observed plants, including their fitted deviations.
Use `appraise()` to assess whether the Gamma response distribution and shared
concentration curve describe the observations adequately.

```{r plant-diagnostics}
appraise(plant_tmb, type = "quantile", seed = 73)
```

The lowest quantile score stands out below the normal reference: one
measurement is substantially lower than its fitted distribution would
typically produce. Inspect the fitted curve for that plant to see whether
other measurements show a similar departure.
[Read smooth effects, interactions and surfaces](smooth-effects.html)
explores more flexible plant-specific curves.

The check above holds the fitted plant effects and smooth fixed. With
`conditioning = "marginal"`, glmmTMB instead simulates new plant effects
**and new spline random coefficients**. That checks the distribution of both
plant variation and the shared curve. See the
[diagnostics article](model-checking.html) for choosing between these checks
and posterior predictive checks. The `glmmTMB-methods` help topic lists supported
response families, model components and current restrictions.
